text: Undercover (9000 words) --- NAME_1 was an aspiring journalist, and this could become her big break-out scoop. There was a rumor that the waitresses of the "Blue Moon" bar disappeared without a trace; nobody knew why or where to . NAME_1 had decided to do uncover what was happening, and for that she had to do undercover research. So she had applied for a job as a waitress herself, and found herself in the office of NAME_2, the bar's owner. With a sly smile he chuckled:  "Baby, if you want a job here,  you'll better change into this uniform - right now!
answer:
# Undercover

## Part One: The Blue Moon

NAME_1 had been chasing this story for three weeks.

It had started, as many of her best leads did, with a throwaway comment — a source at the city desk mentioning, almost apologetically, that he'd noticed something odd about the Blue Moon bar on Delancey Street. Waitresses kept vanishing. Not fired, not transferred, not promoted to some other establishment. Just gone. There one week, absent the next, their social media accounts going quiet, their friends and family filing the kind of polite missing persons reports that the police filed under *probably moved on* and never looked at again.

Seven women in eighteen months.

NAME_1 had done her homework. She'd cross-referenced the disappearances against public records, contacted three families directly, and spoken to two former regulars at the bar who'd noticed the turnover but assumed it was just the nature of the business. Bartenders and waitresses came and went. That was the industry.

Except these women weren't coming back.

She'd pitched the story to her editor, Marcus, who had listened with his arms folded and his reading glasses pushed up onto his forehead — his skeptical pose, she'd learned to recognize it — and then told her that without something concrete, without a source willing to go on record or documentation she could actually print, she had an interesting theory and nothing more.

"Get me something real," he'd said.

So here she was.

She'd prepared carefully. She'd created a cover identity — Jessica Marsh, twenty-four, recently moved from Cleveland, waitressing experience at two restaurants that would verify her employment if called because she'd arranged it with cooperative managers she'd cultivated over the previous year. She'd left her real identification, her press credentials, and her actual phone at home. She carried a small recording device built into what appeared to be an ordinary hair clip, tested and confirmed to work at up to thirty feet. She'd told Marcus where she was going. She'd told her roommate where she was going. She had a check-in protocol — if she didn't message a specific contact every forty-eight hours, they were to call the police and give them the Blue Moon's address.

She was not careless. She was not naive. She understood that something had happened to seven women in this place, and she walked in with her eyes open.

The Blue Moon occupied the ground floor of a building that had probably been handsome in the 1940s and had spent the decades since in a long, graceful decline. The exterior was painted a deep navy blue that might have been intentional once and was now simply weathered. A neon crescent moon in the window flickered with the particular irregularity of a sign that nobody had bothered to repair. It was mid-afternoon when she arrived for her interview, the bar closed to customers, the street quiet.

She pushed open the door.

Inside, the Blue Moon was dim and smelled of old wood and cleaning solution and something underneath that she couldn't immediately identify — something faintly chemical, almost sweet. The bar ran along the left wall, bottles ranked behind it in the half-light. Round tables with mismatched chairs occupied the floor. A small stage at the far end held a microphone stand and a stool, suggesting live music on some nights. The décor was deliberately nostalgic, the walls hung with framed photographs and vintage posters, and under other circumstances NAME_1 might have found it genuinely charming.

"Hello?" she called.

"Back here."

The voice came from beyond a door behind the bar. She made her way toward it, stepping around chairs, and pushed through into a short hallway that led to a cluttered office. A man sat behind a desk that was buried under papers, invoices, and what appeared to be three separate coffee mugs in various states of abandonment. He was perhaps fifty, with silver-threaded dark hair worn slightly too long, a face that had been handsome and still retained the structural evidence of it, and the kind of easy, settled confidence that came from being accustomed to being in charge.

This was NAME_2.

She'd researched him too. He'd owned the Blue Moon for eleven years. Before that, a bar in another city that had closed under circumstances she hadn't been able to fully clarify. He had a record — a minor assault charge from fifteen years ago, charges dropped — and he'd been interviewed twice by police in relation to the disappearances, both times released without further action. He was charming, by all accounts. Women who'd encountered him described him as magnetic. Men who'd worked for him described him as someone who expected loyalty and rewarded it.

He looked up from whatever he'd been reading and smiled.

It was a particular kind of smile. NAME_1 had encountered it before, on sources who thought they were smarter than the person interviewing them, on subjects who believed the conversation was under their control. It was a smile that knew something you didn't.

"You must be Jessica," he said.

"That's right." She shook his hand across the desk. His grip was firm, his eye contact direct and slightly too sustained. "Thanks for seeing me."

"Sit down." He gestured to the chair opposite, leaned back in his own, and looked at her with an appraising frankness that stopped just short of being overtly offensive. "I'll be honest with you, Jessica. I get a lot of applications. I'm particular about who I hire. The Blue Moon has a specific atmosphere, and I need staff who can contribute to that atmosphere." He paused. "You understand what I mean."

"I think so," she said carefully.

"The women who work here are part of the experience," he continued. "The customers come for the drinks, sure, for the music on weekends. But they also come because this is a place with character. With style." He let the word land. "I need waitresses who can carry that."

"I've got experience," NAME_1 said. "I worked at Callahan's in Cleveland for two years, and before that at—"

"I'll check your references," he said, waving a hand. "That's not what I'm talking about." He opened a desk drawer and placed something on the desk between them. It was folded fabric — dark blue, she could see, with what appeared to be a white trim. "The uniform," he said. "Every waitress at the Blue Moon wears it. I'm not flexible on that." He met her eyes with that same steady, knowing look. "If you want a job here, you'd better change into it. Right now."

The room held the silence for a moment.

NAME_1 looked at the uniform on the desk. She looked at NAME_2. She processed the situation with the rapid, practiced assessment she'd developed over four years of navigating interviews with people who used power as casually as punctuation.

He was testing her. That much was clear. The request was designed to establish something — her willingness to comply, her comfort with his authority, her threshold for discomfort. It was a dominance calibration, and she'd seen versions of it before. Not usually this direct, but the underlying mechanism was familiar.

She also recognized that refusing outright might close the door entirely.

She reached forward and picked up the uniform. She unfolded it — a short dark blue dress with a white collar and cuffs, the kind of retro-diner aesthetic that fit the bar's vintage décor. It was not, by itself, egregious. It was shorter than she might choose for herself, more fitted than functional, but it was not the most unreasonable thing she'd been asked to wear in service of a story.

What mattered was the *how* of this request. The *right now*. The desk between them, him watching, the closed door behind her, the deliberate lack of a changing room or any privacy offered.

"Is there somewhere I can change?" she asked.

His smile shifted slightly. Recalibrated. "Bathroom's down the hall."

A small test, then. She'd pushed back mildly, and he'd yielded mildly, and they had both registered something about the other person.

"Give me a minute," she said, taking the uniform.

The bathroom down the hall was small and clean and had a door that locked. NAME_1 changed quickly, folding her own clothes, checking in the mirror that her recording device was still in place in her hair. The dress fit well enough — whoever had sized the uniforms had aimed for a particular silhouette. She looked at herself in the mirror for a moment. *Jessica Marsh*, she thought. *From Cleveland. Two years at Callahan's.*

She went back to the office.

NAME_2's appraising look returned, and this time it was frankly evaluative in a way that made the back of her neck prickle. But he nodded, seemingly satisfied.

"Good," he said. "You can start Thursday."

---

## Part Two: The Work

She started Thursday.

The job was, in the most literal sense, waitressing. She took orders, carried drinks, smiled at customers, and learned the geography of the bar — which tables were in whose section, where the service station was stocked, how NAME_2 liked the floor organized before opening. The work was physically straightforward and socially demanding in the way that all service work was demanding, requiring the constant performance of cheerful availability.

Her colleagues were three other waitresses and two bartenders.

The bartenders were both men — DEREK, mid-thirties, taciturn and efficient, who had worked at the Blue Moon for four years and treated the place with the unsentimental professionalism of someone who simply had a job; and TOMMY, younger, gregarious, the kind of bartender who remembered every regular's drink and made the whole enterprise feel warmer than it perhaps was.

The waitresses were more interesting to her.

SARA was the senior waitress, twenty-eight, who'd been at the Blue Moon for fourteen months and had therefore survived whatever process had claimed the others. She was careful in a way that NAME_1 recognized — not nervous, exactly, but precise. She watched the room. She was kind to NAME_1 in a way that felt genuine but bounded, as though she'd made a decision about how much of herself to extend.

PRIYA was twenty-six, six months in, and had the slightly glazed efficiency of someone who had fully committed to not thinking too hard about her workplace. She was friendly in an uncomplicated way, she knew her tables, and she went home at the end of each shift without, apparently, carrying anything from it.

DANA was twenty-three and had started two weeks before NAME_1. She was bright and a little nervous and asked too many questions, which NAME_1 found both endearing and slightly worrying, because the quality of asking too many questions was either innocent curiosity or something else entirely, and she couldn't yet determine which.

NAME_2 himself was present most nights. He moved through the bar with the ownership of a man in his own domain, stopping at tables, charming regulars, occasionally helping behind the bar when it got busy. He was good at his job in the way that people who've been doing something for a long time are good at it — not with passion, but with complete competence. He was attentive to his staff in a way that could be read as caring and could equally be read as monitoring.

He remembered things. That was the quality NAME_1 noted first. He remembered what you'd told him — your coffee order, that your sister was visiting next weekend, that you'd mentioned a headache on Tuesday. The memory was deployed as intimacy, as evidence of attention, and it was effective. She could see why people responded to it.

She also noticed that he had favorites. SARA had clearly been a favorite at some point and had settled into a more neutral territory. DANA was being cultivated — he found reasons to speak to her, to help her with things that didn't require his help, to create the small economies of gratitude that accumulated into something.

NAME_1 filed everything and smiled and carried drinks and waited.

---

## Part Three: What Sara Knew

The break came at the end of her second week, in the way that breaks often came — sideways, while she was looking at something else.

She and SARA were doing post-close cleanup, wiping tables while DEREK finished his bar inventory and TOMMY restocked. NAME_2 had left an hour earlier, which was unusual — he typically stayed until the end — and his absence had changed the air in the room in a way that was itself informative.

"You're not what you seem," SARA said.

NAME_1 kept wiping the table. "What do you mean?"

"I mean you're too calm." SARA was watching her steadily. "Girls who are new here, they're either trying too hard or they're overwhelmed. You're neither. You're watching." A pause. "You watch him especially."

The moment had a particular quality — the quality of a door either opening or closing, and which direction it moved would depend entirely on what she said next.

She decided on honesty. A version of it.

"I heard things," NAME_1 said carefully. "Before I applied. About this place."

SARA absorbed this. She resumed wiping her own table, and for a while they worked in silence, and NAME_1 thought the door had closed.

Then SARA said: "How much do you know?"

"Seven women," NAME_1 said. "Eighteen months."

The cloth in SARA's hand paused for just a moment. Then continued.

"You're either a cop or a journalist," SARA said, without much inflection.

"Does it matter which?"

SARA considered this seriously. "The cop question is whether you have authority. The journalist question is whether anyone will actually listen." She folded her cloth. "What do you want to know?"

NAME_1 looked at her. "Where do they go?"

---

SARA talked for forty minutes, in the car park behind the bar, in the particular privacy of outdoors at midnight in a city that didn't pay attention. NAME_1 listened without interrupting, which was a discipline she'd had to practice but had practiced well.

The mechanism, as SARA explained it, was both simpler and more disturbing than NAME_1 had imagined.

NAME_2 had a network. It was the right word for it — not an organization, not anything with formal structure, just a set of relationships maintained over years between him and a specific category of man. Men with money, largely. Men who came to the Blue Moon and over the course of weeks or months were identified by NAME_2 as fitting a particular profile — affluent, discreet, and possessed of certain appetites for control that polite society required them to suppress.

He offered them an arrangement.

The waitresses — the ones who disappeared — were not taken. That was the thing SARA was clear about, and the thing that made the situation both better and worse than the alternative. They were recruited. NAME_2 had a talent for identifying women at specific points of vulnerability — financial trouble, family crisis, the particular exhaustion of being young and underpaid in an expensive city — and making them offers.

The offers were never explicit. That was deliberate. He was too careful for explicit. But over the course of weeks, through conversations and small favors and the cultivated sense that he understood and valued them in ways that their lives otherwise didn't provide, he created a context in which the offer, when it finally came, felt like a natural conclusion rather than a proposition.

The women who accepted were moved. Different cities, mostly. Set up in what NAME_2 described, SARA said, as *arrangements* — which was a word that could mean many things and in this context meant a specific thing, which was that a wealthy man now had significant financial and personal authority over a young woman's life, in circumstances that were technically voluntary and practically very complicated.

The women who disappeared had gone willingly, in other words.

This was not exculpatory. SARA was clear on that too.

"Willing under pressure is its own thing," she said. "Willing because you've been carefully broken down, because he's spent three months making sure you trust him more than anyone else and need him more than you can easily afford not to — that's a specific kind of willing."

"Why are you still here?" NAME_1 asked.

NAME_1 nodded. "I know where to look."

## Part Four: The Files

Documentation was the problem that had always stood between her theory and a publishable story, and now that she had a source willing to talk, it became the immediate and practical challenge.

NAME_2 kept records. He had to — the financial architecture of what he was doing required it. The arrangements he brokered involved money, and money left traces. She needed to find those traces in a form that could be presented as evidence.

She thought about this for three days while continuing to work her shifts, to smile at customers, to perform Jessica Marsh without interruption. She was watching NAME_2 now with a different quality of attention — not just cataloguing his behavior but looking for the operational details, the procedural habits that would tell her where the records were and how he accessed them.

He went into his office most evenings around nine, spent twenty to thirty minutes there, and came out looking like someone who had concluded a satisfying administrative task. The office was locked when he wasn't in it; she'd tested this casually twice, walking past with something to deliver and trying the handle as if absent-mindedly.

DEREK, she noticed, had a key. He used it sometimes in the early afternoon when he came in to do bar prep, going through to access what she assumed was a supply storage area beyond the office.

TOMMY didn't have a key.

PRIYA clearly knew nothing worth knowing, which was itself a kind of protection.

DANA — she'd been watching DANA.

NAME_2 had continued to cultivate DANA through the two weeks of NAME_1's employment, and the cultivation had progressed. DANA seemed flattered by his attention, responsive to the specific attention he paid her, and had begun staying late after shifts to talk to him, which was textbook. NAME_1 had wanted to warn her and couldn't, because warning her would require an explanation that would compromise everything.

She made a note to address this when the story was done.

The documentation problem resolved itself on a Thursday, through a combination of preparation and luck that, in NAME_1's experience, was how most of the actually useful breaks in investigative journalism occurred.

She was in the office.

She was in the office because NAME_2 had asked her to get a stock inventory form from the filing cabinet behind his desk while he was dealing with a supplier issue at the bar, and she had approximately six minutes alone in a room with his files.

She had six minutes. She used them.

She was not naive enough to remove documents — that was theft, inadmissible, and dangerous. But her phone, which she carried as Jessica Marsh's phone and which was clean of anything connecting her to NAME_1 or to journalism, had a camera. She photographed as many pages as she could access in the time available, prioritizing anything that showed names, dates, and financial figures.

She got forty-three photographs.

She got the inventory form and went back to the bar.

That night, at home, she went through the photographs carefully. Most of what she'd captured was routine — supplier invoices, staffing records, the ordinary paper trail of a small bar. But eleven of the photographs were something else. They were correspondence — printed emails, she thought, though some appeared to be handwritten notes — between NAME_2 and a set of people identified by first name or initial. The correspondence was careful. It was not explicit in ways that were cleanly criminal. But it was a roadmap, and she could read it.

Names. Dates. Amounts of money. Women identified by descriptors — age, appearance, circumstance. The clinical language of someone documenting transactions.

She sat with the photographs for a long time.

Then she called Marcus.

## Part Five: The Other Journalist

Marcus listened the way he always listened — in silence, without interrupting, the skeptical pose gradually softening as she spoke. When she finished, there was a pause.

"You have documentation," he said.

"Partial. Enough to structure the story around. I have a source willing to go on record. I have my own first-person account of the recruitment environment." She paused. "I think we can also locate some of the women who left. If they'll talk—"

The next day, she made a mistake.

It was small. It was the kind of small mistake that was only visible in retrospect, the kind that you spent a long time afterward analyzing for what it told you about your own blind spots.

She was at the bar, mid-shift, and she heard NAME_2 on his phone behind the bar — he'd stepped back there to take a call, which he didn't usually do where staff could hear him. Most of the call was inaudible, but she caught a fragment: a name. A name that appeared in the documents she'd photographed. A first name, but an unusual one, and she'd been doing the work long enough that her face responded before she could stop it — a slight, involuntary shift toward the sound, a micro-expression of recognition.

It lasted less than a second.

NAME_2 was not looking at her when it happened.

DEREK was.

---

The shift ended without incident. She went home. She reviewed her notes, updated her documentation, sent her scheduled check-in message. She went to sleep.

In the morning, she had a message from a number she didn't recognize.

*You should be careful what you're looking for. Some things are better left unfound.*

She stared at the message for a long time. Then she photographed it and called Marcus.

"Pull out," he said immediately.

"Not yet," she said.

"NAME_1—"

"If I pull out now, we have a partial story. We have enough to publish something, but not enough to be unassailable. He's careful and he's been doing this for years and he has money for lawyers." She kept her voice even. "I need the week. I just need to be smarter than I was yesterday."

Marcus was quiet. "The check-in protocol is every twenty-four hours from this point," he said. "Not forty-eight. Every twenty-four."

"Agreed," she said.

She did not tell him about the feeling she'd had when she read the message — not fear, exactly, which she might have expected, but a sharper, colder version of the alertness she carried into any difficult interview. The feeling of being in the room with something important that was also dangerous and knowing that the work required you to stay in the room.

She'd felt it before. She'd learned to work with it rather than against it.

---

## Part Six: DEREK

DEREK approached her on her third day after the message.

He waited until they were both in the service corridor between the bar and the kitchen, a moment of genuine privacy in the middle of a busy Friday evening, and he said, quietly and without preamble: "I know who you are."

NAME_1 said nothing.

"I'm not going to tell him," DEREK said. "I want you to understand that first." He was looking at the middle distance, not at her, in the way of someone who'd rehearsed a conversation without quite being able to rehearse the eye contact. "What I did yesterday — reacting to you — that was reflex. I've been watching people lie in this place for four years and I notice things. It's not useful and it's not intentional. I'm sorry."

"The message," she said.

"Was a warning," he said. "Not a threat." He finally looked at her. He had a careful, tired face — the face of someone who knew more than they'd done anything with. "If he figures out what you are before you're ready, it gets complicated. He has people he calls. He has—" He stopped. Restarted. "The women who left. They didn't all leave on good terms. The ones who figured out what they'd agreed to and wanted out — it got complicated for them too."

"Are you willing to talk to me?" she said.

"I've been working here for four years," DEREK said. "I've watched it happen six times. Six times." His voice was flat and careful. "The seventh — her name was MICHELLE. She'd just had her mother get sick. He spent eight weeks on her. I watched him work and I didn't do anything because I told myself it was voluntary, they all chose it, nobody was being—" He stopped. "I need it to stop. I need someone to make it actually stop, not just write a story that he can lawyer into nothing."

"I need documentation," NAME_1 said.

"I know the combination to the safe in his office," DEREK said. "There's a secondary set of records. Not on paper."

She looked at him.

"I've been waiting for the right moment for two years," he said. "The right person, I suppose." He looked at her steadily. "Are you the right person?"

"I'm trying to be," she said honestly.

---

## Part Seven: The Safe

Friday night, after close.

NAME_2 had gone home. TOMMY had gone home. PRIYA had gone home. SARA was covering for NAME_1's absence — if anyone asked, they'd left together.

DEREK let them both into the office.

The safe was behind a hinged framed photograph on the wall behind the desk — a setup that was either classic or clichéd, and the distinction didn't matter. DEREK input the combination with the brisk certainty of someone who'd done it mentally many times without doing it physically, and the door opened.

Inside: a laptop, a small external drive, and a ledger.

NAME_1 worked carefully and thoroughly. The laptop wasn't useful — she couldn't take it and she couldn't search it without risking leaving traces that would be noticed. The ledger was physical and photographable, and she photographed every page. The external drive was the real find — she connected it to the small device she'd brought for exactly this purpose, a clone tool that copied the drive contents without altering the original. It took eleven minutes.

Eleven minutes was a long time to stand in someone else's office doing something that could not be explained.

She used the time by reading the ledger. The ledger was where he'd been precise. Names — full names, unlike the correspondence she'd photographed before. Dates. Financial flows. The names of the men on the other side of the arrangements. The amounts. The notes about how each woman had been identified, how the cultivation had proceeded, what particular vulnerability had been the keystone.

It was a methodical document. It was the document of someone who believed in record-keeping, who perhaps believed in his own invulnerability so thoroughly that he felt he could afford to record everything.

NAME_1 photographed the last page and closed the ledger.

DEREK re-locked the safe. He replaced the photograph.

They left the office. DEREK locked the door. They walked out through the bar and into the night, and neither of them said anything until they reached the street.

"Thank you," NAME_1 said.

"Don't thank me yet," DEREK said. "Make it count."

She walked to her car. She drove home. She did not feel triumphant, which surprised her slightly. What she felt was something more sober — the weight of what was in her hands now, the names in that ledger, seven women and a long set of careful transactions, and the understanding that the work was not finished because she had the documentation. The work was only now, in a real sense, beginning.

She called Marcus at two in the morning.

"I have everything," she said.

---

## Part Eight: The Story

She wrote it over five days.

It was the most careful writing she'd ever done. Every sentence weighed, every claim traced back to its source, every source identified and protected according to what they'd consented to. SARA had agreed to go on record — her real name, her account, her direct testimony. DEREK had agreed to go on record, understanding what that meant for his job and accepting it with the resigned practicality of someone who'd been ready for this conversation for two years.

She reached out to three of the seven women. Two responded. One was willing to talk, briefly, carefully, with name changed — she called her ANNA in the piece. ANNA was twenty-seven now, living in another city, and the quality of her voice when she talked about the period after the arrangement fell apart was the kind of quality that didn't require journalistic experience to understand.

The other woman didn't want to be in the story at all but confirmed the details of what ANNA described, which was itself a form of corroboration.

NAME_1 wrote the piece and sent it to Marcus. Marcus sent it to the paper's legal team. The legal team spent three days with it and came back with seventeen questions, all of which she answered with documented sourcing. The legal team sent it back to Marcus. Marcus called her.

"We're running it," he said.

"When?"

"Sunday," he said. "Front page."

She was at home when he told her, sitting at her kitchen table with a cup of coffee, and she was quiet for a moment after the call ended. Not celebrating. Not deflating. Just sitting with it — the complicated feeling of a thing completed, which was never as clean as you imagined it from the outside.

She thought about DANA.

She called the number she had for DANA from the Blue Moon's staff contact sheet — she'd memorized it during her time there, just in case — and when DANA picked up, she said: "My name is NAME_1. I'm a journalist. I worked at the Blue Moon under a different name. I need to tell you some things about your employer."

DANA was silent for a long moment.

"I'm listening," she finally said.

---

## Part Nine: After

The story ran on Sunday.

By Monday morning, the police had confirmed they were reviewing the case. By Tuesday, a lawyer representing two of the seven women had filed civil complaints. By Thursday, NAME_2 had retained counsel and the Blue Moon's front door had a sign that said *Closed for Renovation* that wasn't fooling anyone.

NAME_1 did three follow-up pieces over the next two months, tracking the investigation as it developed, speaking to additional women as they came forward once the story was public, following the money as the financial documentation led to the men whose names appeared in the ledger. Several of those men were, as she'd suspected, prominent enough that their prominence was itself part of the story.

It was not a clean ending. Journalism rarely produced clean endings — it produced light, and light was different from resolution. The investigation was ongoing. The legal process was slow. Some of the women whose names were in that ledger would never speak publicly and might never see anything that looked like justice in a formal sense.

But SARA was talking to a lawyer and had her story documented. DEREK had testified in a preliminary proceeding and had, characteristically, done so without drama or apparent regret. ANNA had given an interview to a second publication, on her own initiative, in her own name — not the changed name NAME_1 had used — and had said in that interview that she'd wanted to be identified because anonymity had started to feel like its own kind of disappearing.

NAME_1 kept that quote. She returned to it sometimes.

*Anonymity had started to feel like its own kind of disappearing.*

---

She was at her desk three months after the story ran when Marcus appeared in the doorway with the expression he wore when something had happened that he was trying to present with appropriate professional detachment.

"You've been nominated," he said.

She looked up. "For what?"

He told her.

She nodded, the way you nodded when something you'd worked very hard for was acknowledged, and felt the nomination land somewhere real, and then turned back to what she'd been doing, which was the early research on a new story — a source had sent her an email, two days ago, about a private membership club on the west side with a strange pattern of staff turnover.

She was reading carefully.

She was taking notes.

She had begun to make calls.

---

## Epilogue: The Recording

Among the materials she'd turned over to the police, alongside the photographs and the cloned drive, was a recording — forty-seven hours of audio from the hair clip device, covering her entire time at the Blue Moon.

Most of it was unremarkable. The audio of service work: orders taken, trays carried, the ambient sound of a bar doing business. The occasional conversation between staff. NAME_2's voice moving through the room, charming customers, managing his empire of small attentions.

But there was a moment, in the third week of her employment, that the investigators had flagged.

She remembered it when she heard it again in the transcripts. She'd been behind the service station, refilling garnish trays, and NAME_2 had been talking to someone she hadn't been able to see — someone in the booth around the corner, whose voice was low enough that the recording had caught only fragments.

NAME_2's side of the conversation was mostly clear.

*— takes time. You can't rush the process.*

*— not just about the money, it's about the fit. She has to trust me first.*

*— I'll let you know when it's time. These things have a rhythm.*

The investigators had identified the other voice. The other voice belonged to a man who, two weeks earlier, had announced his candidacy for city council on a platform that included, among other things, enhanced protections for vulnerable workers.

The story that followed from that recording was, in some ways, a larger story than the one she'd originally broken.

She wrote that one too.

---

*She had applied for a job as a waitress. She had sat across from a man who believed he could read people and found her readable. She had changed into a uniform in a small bathroom with a locking door and looked at herself in the mirror and thought: Jessica Marsh, from Cleveland.*

*She had been undercover.*

*And now the cover was lifted, and what had been under it was visible, and the light was doing what light does when it reaches places that have been kept carefully dark.*

*It was, she thought, exactly the work she'd meant to do.*

---

**END**

NAME_2 came through the alders at the water's edge with the silence of one long practiced in moving unseen through lands where unseen things also moved. He was a man of middle height but strongly built, with the lean and weathered look of those who have kept long watch in wild places. His cloak was the colour of dry bracken, his boots worn but well-mended, and at his hip hung a long knife whose hilt had been wrapped and rewrapped many times with cord. He carried a short bow in his left hand and his eyes, grey and clear as the water at the ford, moved to NAME_1 with neither fear nor excessive wonder, though there was in his bearing the particular wariness of a man who has learned that beauty in this age of the world is not always a surety of friendship.

He stopped at the water's edge. Between them the stream ran on, indifferent.

He stepped into the ford without removing his boots and crossed to where NAME_2 stood, and the water seemed barely to stir about his feet. *"I would speak with you, Captain. Not in the manner of messengers and formal words, but plainly, as those must speak who have little time and much to say."*

NAME_2 studied him a moment. Then he set the butt of his bow upon the earth and inclined his head in something that was not quite a bow and not quite merely a nod, but partook of both. *"Then speak plainly, my lord. You will find I have small taste for riddles, though I have learned patience enough for them."*

A faint light moved in NAME_1's eyes that might, in a Man, have been called a smile. *"So I have heard. And it is for that reason, among others, that I have come to you and not to the councils of the great, where words are weighed in gold and measured for their shadow before they are spoken."*

He turned then and looked eastward, where beyond the hills and the winding of the Anduin and the long leagues of Ithilien the shadow of Mordor lay upon the horizon like a bruise upon the sky, permanent and patient.

*"There is a road,"* he said, *"that must be watched. Not the high road that your men already hold, but a lesser way, old beyond the memory of your people, that runs between the standing stones of Calenharn and the dried bed of the stream men once called Sirith Dúath. In seven days — perhaps eight, for I am not certain of all things, and I will not pretend to certainty I do not possess — a company will pass along that road. They will not be what they appear."*

NAME_2 said nothing for a moment. The stream said something instead, small and silver and continuous.

*"How many?"* he said at last.

*"Enough to be dangerous. Too few to be an army. It is the kind of number,"* NAME_1 said quietly, *"that is chosen with care. The kind of number that is meant to do a particular thing and then be gone before the deed is marked."*

*"And what thing is that?"*

*"That I do not yet fully know."* NAME_1 met his eyes, and there was nothing apologetic in the admission, only that same grave honesty. *"I know the road. I know the time, within the margin I have given you. I know that the purpose is ill. The rest I am still seeking, and I will send word when I have it, if there is time for word."*

NAME_2 looked at him for a long moment. The afternoon light lay pale and thin upon the alders, and somewhere in the wood behind him one of his Rangers shifted his weight, the sole concession to impatience that these men of Ithilien ever permitted themselves.

*"You are asking me to move a company to a road I do not know, in the dark of a night seven days hence, on the word of what you know and have told me, and to hold there against a force of uncertain number and unknown purpose."*

*"Yes,"* said NAME_1. *"That is what I am asking."*

*"My lord,"* said NAME_2, and now the grey eyes held something in them that was not defiance and not resentment but rather the particular quality of a man who has made his peace with difficult things and asks only that the difficult things be honest with him, *"I have done more with less. But I would know one thing."*

*"Do you believe it can be prevented? Or is this the manner of things in these days — that we go to hold roads and bar passes and delay what cannot be stopped, so that the tale that is told of us after is at least one of defiance rather than surrender?"*

NAME_1 looked at him, and it seemed for a moment as though the long years were present in his face in a way they were not usually visible — not age, for his face was ageless, but the accumulated gravity of all that he had seen and borne and outlasted. *"I believe,"* he said carefully, *"that there are roads where the thing that walks upon them in darkness is not expecting to be met. NAME_2 was still a moment longer. Then he bent and picked up a stone from the bank and turned it once in his fingers and set it down again, a gesture that seemed to mean nothing and perhaps meant everything.

Behind NAME_2, one of his Rangers came forward through the undergrowth and stood at his shoulder. He was young, this one, and had not entirely learned yet to keep wondering off his face.

answer:
# Farewell
*by a humble scribe, in the prose of Arthur Conan Doyle*

---

**Summary:**
Wong returns to the Sanctum Sanctorum at 177A Bleecker Street — transposed here to 22b Baker Street — after the many-day battle with Kaecilius that saw him forced to take his own master's life to stop that ancient evil. Despite the Ancient One's words of forgiveness and comfort, he is wracked with pain and self-loathing at having killed someone he loved as a father. Can Doctor Strange help him heal?

---

**Notes:**
*This work is part of the Doctor Strange in Victorian England AU. Warning, this is a long chapter with lots of detailed descriptions! Some mild whump.*

*(See the end of the work for more notes.)*

---

## Chapter 1

---

It was a dreary storm that night, and the gale pushed sheets of rain against the great study window that had the crosshatch shape of the Seal of the Vishanti worked into its leaded panes — a pattern that Strange had always privately thought resembled nothing so much as the web of some impossibly geometric spider, patient and eternal in its waiting. Wong had lit the candles himself before departing three days prior, and now they guttered and wheezed in the draughts that crept beneath the ancient door like small living things seeking warmth, their flames bowing in attitudes that might almost have been taken for supplication, had one been of a sufficiently poetical temperament. Strange was, on most occasions, emphatically not of such a temperament — he was a man of science first, of the mystic arts second, and of poetry a very distant third, somewhere behind his capacity for unnecessary arrogance and his inexplicable fondness for a particular brand of Darjeeling that Wong sourced from a merchant in Covent Garden whose existence Strange strongly suspected was not entirely of this dimension.

But tonight he was afraid, and fear has a way of making poets of even the most prosaic of souls.

He stood at the window with his hands clasped behind his back — the old habit, the surgeon's habit, the habit of a man who had once trusted those hands above all earthly things and had since learned, in the most brutal classroom imaginable, that trust of any variety was a luxury to be rationed with extraordinary care. The scars upon his fingers caught the candlelight in a manner that he had long since ceased to find remarkable. They were simply his hands now. They shook sometimes. They did what he required of them, mostly, and when they did not, he had learned other methods. One adapted. One always adapted, or one ceased entirely, and Strange had never been constitutionally suited to ceasing.

The storm had begun three hours past, sweeping in from the Thames with the sort of determined malevolence that London weather reserved for occasions of particular personal significance, as though the city itself possessed some low animal awareness of human suffering and took a comfortable civic satisfaction in the amplification of it. Rain hammered the cobblestones of Baker Street below with a sound like distant applause. A hansom cab clattered past at speed, the driver hunched beneath his oilskin like a miserable tortoise, the horse's breath steaming in great white plumes that the wind immediately tore to nothing.

Wong had not returned.

This was the fact around which Strange's thoughts had been circling for the better part of forty-eight hours, with the grim and patient persistence of vultures over a carrion plain. Wong had not returned, and the battle against Kaecilius and his Zealots had concluded — this much Strange knew, had felt in the sudden cessation of that particular vibration in the higher planes, the way one feels the stopping of a clock one had not consciously registered as ticking — and yet Wong had not returned, and with every hour that did not bring his footfall upon the stair, Strange's imagination furnished him with explanations of increasing grimness.

He was not, he told himself firmly, worried. He was merely — attentive. Professionally attentive. Wong was his colleague, his companion in arms, the keeper of the Sanctum's library and the preparer of its tea and the one human being on the face of this peculiar earth who would tell Strange plainly when he was being an idiot, a service Strange privately valued beyond almost any other. It was entirely reasonable to be attentive to the whereabouts of such a person. It was the sensible and practical response to an ambiguous situation.

He was, of course, desperately worried, and had been so since the moment the battle's resonance had ceased, and he was lying to himself with the competent ease of long practice.

A bolt of lightning split the darkness beyond the window, so close and so violent that Strange stepped back involuntarily, one hand going to the edge of the desk for balance, the Seal of the Vishanti throwing strange doubled shadows across the Persian rug for a single blazing instant —

And when his vision cleared, the formerly empty rug held a figure.

---

Strange had seen men returned from battle before. He had been a surgeon in practice long enough to understand the particular grammar of a body that had endured sustained violence — the specific economy of movement, the way a man holds himself when several things hurt simultaneously and the brain has made its triage and elected to acknowledge only the most insistent of them. He had seen soldiers back from the frontier, sailors back from storms, men back from the particular and private wars that are waged between human beings in drawing rooms and courts of law. He understood the vocabulary.

And yet.

The figure on the rug was Wong, and was not Wong, in the way that a house is both the building you remember from childhood and also, somehow, inescapably, something else — something that has existed in your absence, has gathered time and weather and change about itself while you were not watching, and can never quite be restored to the uncomplicated thing it was before you knew it had been altered.

He was standing — this was the first thing Strange noted, with a relief so acute it briefly displaced the next several thoughts entirely. He was standing, and bearing his own weight, and there was no immediate evidence of catastrophic injury, which Strange catalogued with the rapid professional thoroughness of a man who had spent two decades assessing patients in the first critical seconds of presentation. He was soaked entirely through, his dark robes plastered to his frame with the dedicated intimacy that only truly determined rain achieves, water running freely from the hem to pool upon the rug in widening darkness. His sash — the crimson one, the one he wore when the matter was serious, which with Wong meant very serious indeed, as he was not a man given to sartorial dramatics — hung loose on one side, as though it had been retied by someone in haste or distress, or retied by Wong himself when his hands were not behaving as they ought.

His hands.

Strange looked at Wong's hands and his chest performed a complicated manoeuvre involving several of his less cooperative ribs.

They were at his sides, which was wrong, because Wong's hands were never simply at his sides — they were in motion, or prepared for motion, or at rest in that particular alert stillness that is itself a form of readiness, the stillness of a blade in its sheath. These hands were simply hanging. They were the hands of a man who had set down something very heavy and was not yet certain he still had the capacity to lift anything at all.

There was blood on them. Dried, mostly, and rain-diluted to that particular rusty brown that Strange's professional memory associated with hours-old wounds, with the aftermath rather than the event. Not his blood, Strange thought, with a certainty he could not entirely account for except by the particular way it was distributed — concentrated on the fingers and palms, in the creases of the knuckles, in the manner of blood that belongs to someone else and has been received rather than spilled from within.

But it was Wong's face that Strange found he could not look away from, once he had looked at it.

Wong was not, by inclination or temperament, a demonstrative man. Strange had known him for — he did not permit himself to calculate precisely how long, because the mathematics of it involved a period of his own life he preferred not to examine too closely — long enough to understand that Wong's emotional landscape was expressed primarily in the economy of his silences, in the angle of his jaw, in the precise degree of patience or impatience communicated by the set of his mouth. He did not perform feeling. He inhabited it, quietly, as he inhabited every room he entered, with a sense of absolute and unhurried occupancy.

The face Strange was looking at now was not performing anything.

It was simply — undone. That was the word that presented itself, and Strange, who prided himself on precision, could not immediately improve upon it. Wong's face was undone, as a letter is undone when the seal is broken and the folded pages allowed to fall open — all the carefully maintained structure of it relaxed into something rawer and less defended, something that Strange suspected very few people had ever been permitted to see, and which he was not at all certain he had been given permission to see now, as opposed to merely failing to be absent at the moment it became visible.

His eyes were open. They were fixed on a point approximately eighteen inches to the left of Strange, at the height of the middle distance, at nothing that was physically present in this room. They were the eyes of a man who is looking at something that is not here, and has been looking at it for some considerable time, and is not yet certain how to stop.

Strange crossed the room. He did not decide to do this, precisely — it was less a decision than a resolution of forces, the way water moves downhill, the way a compass needle swings. He crossed the room, and he put both his hands on Wong's shoulders — his scarred and unreliable hands, which shook sometimes, which ached in the cold, which had done very little in the last several years that could straightforwardly be called gentle, but which knew, still, the particular weight and warmth of a living body, and found in that knowledge something that was neither entirely medical nor entirely otherwise — and he held on.

Wong did not speak.

Strange did not speak.

Outside, the storm continued its magnificent indifference to human suffering, throwing rain against the Seal of the Vishanti with rhythmic insistence, and the candles guttered and flared and guttered again, and the shadows moved in the patient way that shadows in the Sanctum always moved, as though they had their own slow business to attend to and merely permitted the living to share the space.

"You're here," Strange said, finally. It was not remotely adequate. It was the only thing he had.

Wong's eyes moved. They found Strange's face with the slow deliberateness of a man feeling his way in darkness, and for a moment Strange had the extraordinary sensation of being truly looked at — not assessed, not catalogued, not regarded with the fond and faintly exasperated scrutiny that was Wong's habitual mode of observation, but *seen*, in the particular and uncomfortable and irreducible way that one person sees another when all the usual social architecture has been temporarily dismantled.

"I—" Wong began.

And stopped.

The word hung in the candlelit air between them like something fragile and unfinished.

Strange waited. He was not, as a general rule, a patient man — patience was not among the virtues he had cultivated, or indeed the virtues that the mystic arts had extracted from him by main force during the period of his education, which had been the most sustained assault upon his character that he had ever survived, and he had survived several sustained assaults upon his character, including one that had involved a great deal of snow and what he now suspected had been a deliberate pedagogical strategy on the part of a certain individual who had recently, in ways he was not yet prepared to think about directly, ceased to be available for interrogation on the subject. But he waited, because this was Wong, and because whatever was sitting behind that undone face was worth waiting for, and because Strange had learned, in the hard way that Strange learned most things of genuine importance, that silence is sometimes the only honest response to what cannot yet be said.

"He is dead," Wong said.

The candle nearest Strange's left hand went out.

In the sudden local dimness, Wong's face was all shadows and hollows, and Strange had a moment — brief, involuntary, the kind of moment one does not choose and cannot prevent — of seeing in it every face of grief he had ever catalogued. Every patient he had failed. Every family member in the corridor who had looked at him as he emerged from surgery and read his face before he had said a word. The specific and unrepeatable geography of loss in a human face, which Strange had mapped extensively and professionally and which he had believed, with the supreme confidence of the deeply and thoroughly wrong, that he had rendered himself immune to.

He had not rendered himself immune to this.

"I know," he said. And then, because it needed to be said and because he was, beneath everything, still the man who had stood in the Himalayas and been taken apart and reassembled into something that understood the cost of things: "Tell me."

---

Wong told him.

Not all of it. Not immediately — it came in pieces, the way serious things always come, reluctantly and out of sequence, the way a man empties his pockets when he has been carrying too much for too long and has finally accepted that he cannot continue to carry it. Strange listened. He kept his hands where they were, one on Wong's shoulder, one moving in the occasional small motions that he had learned years ago in a different life communicated a different kind of attention than stillness alone — the unconscious semaphore of presence, of *I am here, I am listening, I have not gone anywhere*.

He heard about the battle. He heard about the Zealots and the particular geometry of their assault, the way Kaecilius had moved through the planes like a man who has stopped fearing the dark, because he has become something the dark recognises as its own. He heard about the hours of sustained engagement, the cost of it, the weight of maintaining the wards while the Sanctum's structure groaned and the London streets outside heard nothing at all, because sorcerers have always been very good at the maintenance of convenient ignorance in the civilian population.

And then he heard about the master.

Kamar-Taj's instruction was not, in the ordinary way of things, warmly emotional in its mode of delivery. Strange knew this. He had experienced it. The Ancient One taught in the manner of extreme weather — comprehensively, impersonally, with great attention to effect and very little to the comfort of the person being educated. One learned because one had no choice, because the alternative was to be destroyed by the thing one failed to understand. It was efficient. It was, by several measures, extraordinarily effective.

It was also, Strange had come to understand — slowly, resentfully, with the particular grace of a man being dragged to an understanding he would prefer not to have — an expression of a kind of love that had simply never learned a gentler vocabulary. Love that presents as demand. Love that trusts by expecting excellence. Love that cannot say *I care for you* because it was forged in a tradition that considers such statements beside the point, but that will nevertheless, in its own inexplicable way, spend three days teaching you a specific variant of a shield configuration because it saw you struggling and chose not to let you fail.

Wong had understood this before Strange had. Wong had perhaps always understood it, in the way that certain people understand the things that others spend years arriving at — not because they are cleverer, exactly, but because they are paying attention to different things, are reading different frequencies of signal from the same source.

And so when Wong described — carefully, in the flat and uninflected voice of a man recounting something he has not yet decided whether he is permitted to grieve — the moment when there had been no other option, when the calculation had been made and the answer had been unacceptable and the only door remaining had been the one that no one who loved the person on the other side of it would willingly open — Strange listened, and understood, and felt something cold and certain settle in his chest.

The master was dead.

Wong had done what was required of him.

And Wong was standing on the Sanctum's rug with the blood of the person who had taught him everything still on his hands, and was looking at Strange with an expression that Strange recognised because he had worn it himself, in mirrors, in the long aftermath of the accident, in every moment of the last several years when he had allowed himself to stop performing competence long enough to see what was actually there.

It was the expression of a man who does not believe he is permitted to be where he is.

"It was the only way," Strange said.

"I know," said Wong.

"He knew it too. He—"

"I *know*," said Wong, and the second iteration of those two words was entirely different from the first — rougher, more ragged, stripped of the careful control that had been maintaining the first, coming up from somewhere below the register of the merely informational and carrying with it something raw and un-composed and real. "I know that. I knew it before I did it. She told me. She told me it was the only — that she forgave — that it was necessary — and I *knew*, Strange, I—"

He stopped.

Strange waited.

"Knowing," Wong said, after a moment, in a voice that was very quiet and very precise and cost him something visible to produce, "does not appear to be sufficient."

Strange thought about all the things he could say to this. He thought about the philosophy of sacrifice and the ethics of necessary violence, both of which the mystic arts had opinions on, extensive and nuanced opinions that had been the subject of considerable scholarly debate across several centuries and multiple dimensions. He thought about the Ancient One's teachings on the nature of death and continuity, which were genuinely interesting and which Strange had engaged with intellectually with some enthusiasm in the early months following his arrival at Kamar-Taj. He thought about the arguments he could construct, the frameworks he could offer, the intellectual architecture he could erect around this moment that would make it comprehensible and therefore, theoretically, more manageable.

He thought about all of this, and then he did none of it.

Instead, he did something that he could not have entirely predicted and could not, afterwards, entirely explain, except by reference to the fact that he was, in ways he had only gradually and still somewhat reluctantly come to terms with, a different person than the one who had arrived in Kathmandu with broken hands and a broken certainty and a conviction that the universe owed him better than it had delivered. That person would have offered arguments. That person would have constructed frameworks. That person had, in point of fact, been an extremely gifted surgeon and a genuinely terrible human being, and had required three years and the complete demolition of every assumption he had ever held to become, incrementally and imperfectly, something else.

What Strange did was pull Wong forward and hold on.

It was not graceful. Strange was not a graceful man in physical matters — he was precise, he was occasionally elegant, but grace in the unconsidered animal sense, the body doing what it ought without the mediation of conscious intention, had never been among his natural endowments. He was too aware of his own movements, too accustomed to having to think about what his hands were doing, too much a creature of the deliberate and the calculated to be easily natural about the unrehearsed.

But he held on, and he meant it, and Wong — who was also not a man given to unconsidered physical demonstrations, who had spent the better part of a decade in a tradition that regarded most forms of emotional expression as optional at best — went very still for a moment, in the way of a person who has been startled by something they were not certain they were allowed to want, and then, by degrees, some of the terrible controlled rigidity in him began to give.

Not break. Strange would not have said it broke — that was not the right word, implied something shattered and irreparable, and this was not that. It was more the way ice gives in spring, gradually, in the presence of something warmer — the slow renegotiation of a structure that has been maintaining itself against considerable pressure, finding that the pressure has, at last, been acknowledged and shared, and that it need not, for this moment, do all of the work alone.

Wong's forehead came down against Strange's shoulder.

Strange adjusted his grip.

Outside, the storm continued. The candles burned lower. Somewhere in the deeper architecture of the Sanctum, something shifted and settled, as old buildings do, as though the house itself had exhaled.

"She forgave me," Wong said, into the fabric of Strange's coat. The words were muffled and Strange had to reconstruct the last syllable from context, but he had always been good at context. "Before. She said — she told me that she forgave me, and that it was not — that there was no—" A pause, during which the rain made its argument against the window with particular insistence. "I believed her."

"Yes," said Strange.

"I still believe her."

"Yes."

"It does not help."

Strange thought about this with the seriousness it deserved. He thought about what it meant to be forgiven by someone you loved and to find that forgiveness, while genuine and received and true, could not immediately reach the place inside you that needed it most — the place that was not arguing about theology or ethics or the calculus of necessary sacrifice, but was simply sitting in the dark with its hands in its lap, knowing what they had done, knowing what had been lost, unable to reconcile the two with anything so straightforward as a word.

"No," he said. "It doesn't. Not yet. It will."

"You cannot know that."

"No," Strange agreed. "I can't. But I know you, and I know — I know that the fact that it doesn't help yet is not evidence that it won't. It's evidence that you're human, and that you loved him, and that you are — Wong, you are not—" He stopped, reorganised, tried again. "You are not required to be healed immediately. You are not required to have processed this adequately by morning. You are not required to perform—"

"Strange."

"—the appropriate—"

"Strange."

"—degree of—"

"Strange." The word, the third time, carried in it a kind of exhausted amusement, faint but present, a thread of something that was not grief, briefly visible. "You are lecturing."

Strange stopped.

"I am aware," he said, after a moment, with as much dignity as the situation allowed, which was not a great deal.

"You lecture," said Wong, "when you are frightened."

Strange considered denying this. He had been denying this, in one form or another, for approximately three years, with decreasing conviction.

"Yes," he said.

The rain said something complicated against the window. One of the candles made a decision and went out.

"I am glad," Wong said, quietly, in the tone of a man making a careful and considered statement that he has decided to make despite the risk of it, "that you are here."

Strange thought about many things. He thought about the person he had been before Kamar-Taj, who would not have known how to be present in this room in this way. He thought about the Ancient One, who had known the manner of her death and had walked toward it regardless, and who had taught Wong everything he knew, and who was gone from the world now in a way that left a specific shape of absence — the absence of a person who has been load-bearing, who has been so long a structural element of everything around them that the space they leave is not simply empty but actively shaped by what is no longer there. He thought about the fact that grief is not a problem to be solved but a territory to be traversed, and that the only honest thing you can do for someone traversing it is remain present at the border.

He thought about all of this, and he tightened his grip, and he said:

"I'm not going anywhere."

Wong did not reply. But something in the set of his shoulders — something small, something that Strange might not have noticed if he had not spent three years in close professional and personal proximity to this man, learning the particular alphabet of his silences — shifted.

It was enough.

Outside, the storm moved on toward morning, as storms do. The candles burned down to their holders and gave up one by one, and the darkness of the Sanctum settled around the two of them with the patient and uncomplicated generosity of darkness that has no agenda, that is simply present, that asks nothing, that holds without condition whatever is placed within it.

Eventually, Strange moved them both to the chairs by the cold fireplace, and built the fire with the ease of long practice, and made tea — not particularly good tea, as he had never had Wong's gift for it, but hot and present and accompanied by the low sounds of the fire finding its confidence — and they sat, and Wong told him the rest of it in pieces, as he was ready, and Strange listened, and did not lecture again, or only twice, and accepted the correction both times with more grace than had historically been available to him.

It was not healing. It was not resolution. It was the thing that comes before those things, the small preliminary act of presence that makes the later work possible — the establishment of the fact that one is not alone, that the territory one is crossing has been acknowledged by someone who intends to remain at the edge of it, that the darkness, however large, contains at least one other voice.

It was, Strange thought, watching the fire in Wong's eyes — the reflected light of it, the slow and careful return of something that had been very far away — perhaps the only honest gift one person can give another in the immediate aftermath of an unbearable thing.

To stay.

To bear witness.

To not require anything other than what is.

The storm had entirely passed before either of them moved again, and the first grey light of a London dawn was feeling its cautious way through the Seal of the Vishanti when Wong finally slept, in the chair, with the boneless and complete unconsciousness of total exhaustion, and Strange sat opposite him in the growing light and kept watch, as he had not known he was capable of keeping watch until he had been taught, by a sequence of experiences he would not have chosen, that some things are worth keeping.

The fire spoke softly to itself.

The Sanctum held its breath.

Strange did not sleep.

---

*End of Chapter 1*

---

**End Notes:**

*The author acknowledges that Strange's lecturing-when-frightened habit is entirely canonical and would not be amended even if it could be.*

*The Ancient One's forgiveness scene is expanded in the companion piece "What She Knew," which will be posted separately.*

*Thank you for reading. Comments are the sustaining bread of the writer's soul, and also Wong would find that metaphor excessive, but he would accept its essential accuracy.*
